blocks.p: Start here, because all four devices in the stem are doing the same thing and the answer is incoherent without it. A propeller does not convert all the shaft power it absorbs into useful thrust. Two of the losses are physically recoverable, and both of them are left in the water immediately abaft the propeller - which is exactly where the rudder sits.

ul: Rotational or swirl loss. The propeller imparts a tangential velocity to the race as well as an axial one. That rotating column of water carries real kinetic energy which does nothing for the ship, and it is typically the largest single recoverable loss - of the order of several per cent of delivered power on a conventional single-screw ship.

The hub vortex. Behind the propeller boss there is a low-pressure core into which a concentrated vortex forms. It costs drag, it is a source of cavitation erosion and pressure pulses, and it is entirely wasteful.
Separation and drag on the rudder itself. Not a propeller loss at all, but a loss the rudder introduces - and one that can be reduced by shaping the rudder correctly for the flow it actually meets.

blocks.p: The rudder is the only large appendage standing in the accelerated, swirling slipstream, and it is already there, already structurally supported and already surveyed. That is why so much energy-saving effort has been directed at it. State plainly what follows: a rudder device recovers energy that is already being wasted. It does not create thrust from nothing, and its gain is therefore bounded by the size of the loss it is recovering from.

What it is. A pair of horizontal, wing-like fins projecting from each side of the rudder, set within the propeller slipstream, usually one pair above and one pair below the shaft line, and generally close to the leading edge.

How it works. The flow arriving at the fin is not axial - it carries the propeller's swirl, and above the shaft line the tangential component is in one direction while below it the direction is reversed. Each fin is therefore set at a small angle of attack to its own local flow, and as an aerofoil it develops lift. Because the fin is horizontal, the lift vector is roughly athwartships and its resolved component points forward - that forward component is recovered thrust. Simultaneously the fin straightens the swirl it has taken energy out of, which reduces the residual rotational loss further aft.

Practical points that earn marks. The fins are handed: because the swirl reverses across the shaft line, the upper and lower fins are set at opposite angles, and a fin fitted the wrong way up is a drag device. They are usually combined with a rudder bulb, which carries the fin roots and gives them a sound structural attachment. They add wetted surface and therefore some frictional drag, so the net gain is the recovered thrust minus that penalty. Claimed gains are of the order of 2 to 5 per cent at design condition.

Limitations. The gain falls away off the design draught and speed, because the swirl field and the fin's angle of attack both change. In heavy weather and astern running the fins are loaded in ways they were not optimised for, and their attachment to the rudder must be designed for it.

What it is. A rudder whose section is not the same above and below the propeller shaft line - either twisted, so that the leading edge is turned one way above the shaft and the other way below it, or offset, with the two halves displaced relative to the centreline.

How it works. The reasoning follows directly from section 1. Above the shaft line the swirling race approaches the rudder from one side; below it, from the other. A conventional symmetrical rudder set on the centreline therefore meets an incident angle of attack over almost its entire span, even with the helm amidships. The consequences are continuous lift-induced drag, flow separation, and - most importantly on a modern high-power ship - cavitation on the rudder surface, particularly at the leading edge and around the gap at the horn.

Twisting the leading edge so that each half is aligned with its own local inflow removes the built-in incidence. The result is less separation, less drag, and a rudder that is working with the flow rather than against it. Course-keeping usually improves as well, because the rudder is no longer generating a small standing side force that the helmsman or autopilot must trim out.

Practical points. The twist is designed for one propeller, one direction of rotation and one loading condition, so an asymmetric rudder is not a general-purpose component and cannot simply be transferred between ships. It is frequently combined with a leading-edge bulb and with fins, the three being designed together. It is a newbuilding or major-conversion item rather than a bolt-on retrofit, because the rudder itself is replaced. Claimed gains are of the order of 2 to 6 per cent, and on many installations the cavitation and erosion benefit is the real one - a rudder that stops eroding saves steel repairs and off-hire whether or not the fuel saving is realised.

What it is. A streamlined, roughly axisymmetric body fitted on the leading edge of the rudder, aligned with and close abaft the propeller boss, so that boss and bulb together form a continuous faired body.

How it works. It attacks the hub vortex specifically. The propeller boss ends abruptly, the flow cannot close behind it, and a low-pressure core forms in which the hub vortex is generated. Placing a bulb in that space fills the volume the vortex would occupy and allows the flow to close gradually along a fair body instead of separating. The vortex is suppressed or greatly weakened, and with it go the vortex drag, a source of cavitation erosion on the rudder, and part of the pressure-pulse excitation transmitted into the hull.

Practical points. The gap between boss and bulb, and the alignment, are critical - a bulb that is too far aft or off the shaft axis achieves very little, and the installation tolerance is a real construction issue. The bulb is very commonly the structural base for thrust fins, and the combined arrangement is what most makers actually supply. It is one of the more practicable retrofits, because it can often be added to an existing rudder in dry dock without replacing it. Claimed gains are of the order of 2 to 5 per cent, and are larger on heavily loaded propellers, where the hub vortex is strongest - which also means the benefit is greatest on exactly the ships that suffer most from rudder erosion.

What it is. A freely rotating wheel of larger diameter than the propeller, mounted on the propeller shaft or on its own bearing immediately abaft the propeller, and connected to nothing. It absorbs no shaft power at all.

How it works. This is the most elegant idea of the four and it should be explained in two parts, because the whole device turns on the fact that its blades do two different jobs at two different radii.

ul: The inner portion of the span lies inside the propeller race. There the swirling, accelerated flow drives the blade section round - the wheel is acting as a turbine, extracting rotational energy from the slipstream and using it to spin itself.
The outer portion of the span lies outside the race, in undisturbed water. There the same rotation makes the blade section act as a propeller, generating additional thrust.

The wheel therefore takes wasted rotational energy from the race and converts it into axial thrust in the surrounding water, taking nothing from the engine. It free-wheels at a speed set by the balance between the turbine torque inboard and the propeller torque outboard.

blocks.p: Why it is treated differently from the other three. The stem asks about devices currently in use, and an honest answer distinguishes here. Claimed gains reached about 10 per cent, the highest of any device in this family, and a number of ships were fitted in the 1980s. Service experience was poor. The outer blade span is long, slender and lightly supported, and it runs in a highly unsteady flow at the boundary between the race and the free stream; blade fatigue and blade loss were experienced, along with bearing problems on the free-running hub. A lost blade means severe imbalance on an unrestrained wheel immediately abaft the propeller. The device is consequently rare in service today, and is examined mainly because it demonstrates the principle in its purest form.

blocks.h: 6. What the four have in common, and how they combine

blocks.p: Pull the four together before moving on, because this is where a candidate demonstrates understanding rather than recall.

ul: All four are recovery devices, not power sources. Each takes energy that is already in the water and turns some of it into thrust or removes a drag penalty. None improves the engine, the shafting or the propeller itself.

Three of the four attack rotational energy - fins, twist and the vane wheel all work on the swirl. Only the bulb attacks a different loss, the hub vortex, which is why the bulb combines so well with the others.

The gains do not add. This is the single most important qualification in the answer. A bulb, a pair of fins and a twisted section are all drawing on the same finite pool of wasted energy, so fitting all three does not give the sum of their individually claimed percentages. The combined arrangement must be designed and tested as one system.

They are propeller-and-hull specific. Every one of them is optimised for a particular wake field, propeller, direction of rotation, draught and speed. A device transferred from a sister ship in a different trade will not perform as advertised.

They are permanent appendages with structural and survey consequences. Attachment, welding, fatigue and inspection access have to be considered, and the fitting is examined at the ship's underwater surveys.

blocks.p: For completeness in one sentence, so the examiner sees the boundary: the propeller-side members of the same family - ducts, boss cap fins and pre-swirl stators - attack the same losses from ahead of or on the propeller, and the stem confines this answer to the rudder side.
The stem is set in an Engineering Management paper, so say how the choice is actually made.

ul: Retrofit feasibility. A bulb, and fins on a bulb, are realistic retrofits in a scheduled dry docking. An asymmetric rudder generally is not, because the rudder is replaced; it belongs to a newbuilding or a major conversion.

Operating profile, not design point. The device is optimised at a draught and speed. Judge it against the ship's actual laden and ballast draughts and her actual service speed, which after years of slow steaming is frequently well below the design point at which the gain was calculated.

Do the cheap things first. A fouled hull or a rough, pitted propeller will erase the entire gain of any of these devices, and hull and propeller cleaning costs a fraction of a retrofit. It is difficult to justify an energy saving device on a ship whose hull performance is not already being managed.

Commercial and regulatory driver. At this sitting the pressure is real and current: EEXI and the operational carbon intensity rating have applied since 1 January 2023, and the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy was adopted on 7 July 2023, one month before this examination. A device that improves the attained EEXI or the annual rating has a value beyond the fuel bill.

Structural and class approval. The attachment, the local scantlings and the fatigue assessment need the society's approval, and the rudder's cavitation behaviour after modification should be assessed rather than assumed.
Docking and inspection. Fins and bulbs are exposed appendages. They are damaged by ice, by tugs and by contact, and their condition is a docking survey item.

blocks.h: 8. Judging whether a claimed gain is real

blocks.p: Close on the critical judgement, because this is what separates an engineer's answer from a brochure.

ul: Quoted percentages are almost always model-scale or computational results at the design condition - design draught, design trim, design speed, calm water, clean hull.

Scale effects flatter the model. The wake field and the boundary layer of a model do not scale exactly to full size, and energy saving devices working in the wake are precisely where that error is largest.
The gains of combined devices are not additive, for the reason given in section 6.
The ship rarely operates at the design point. Trim, draught, fouling, weather and part-load running all move her away from it.

Verify in service by measurement, not by assertion. The route is continuous hull and propeller performance monitoring - shaft power against speed through water, corrected for displacement, trim and weather - assessed on the industry standard for measuring changes in hull and propeller performance, ISO 19030, over enough time to separate the device's effect from fouling.
Ask for full-scale before-and-after data from a sister ship in a comparable trade, and treat a maker unable to supply it accordingly.

blocks.p: End on the proposition that governs the whole subject: these devices do not make the ship more powerful - they make her waste less. The gain is bounded by the loss, it is largest where the loss is largest, and it is real only if it can still be measured on the ship a year later.

The stem names four devices and invites four disconnected descriptions. The structure above refuses that: section 1 establishes the two recoverable losses first, and then each device is explained as an attack on one of them. The payoff is visible in section 6 - the candidate can say why the gains do not add, which is a proposition he cannot reach at all if he has described four devices in isolation.

Sections 2 to 5 are deliberately parallel - what it is, how it works, practical points, limitations - so the marker can find each device instantly and so the candidate has a template he can apply under time pressure to a device he half remembers. The parallel structure is also insurance: if time runs short, the last device still gets its two most valuable sentences.

Sections 7 and 8 are what lift this from a naval-architecture answer to an Engineering Management answer. The examiner is a marine engineer and the paper is a management paper; a candidate who can say which of these is a realistic retrofit, and how he would verify a claimed saving in service, has answered the question a Chief Engineer would actually be asked.

ul: Describing four devices without ever saying what energy they are recovering. The loss budget is the answer's spine and without it nothing else can be justified.
Adding the claimed percentages together. A bulb at 4 per cent plus fins at 4 per cent plus a twisted section at 4 per cent is not 12 per cent - all three are drawing on the same wasted energy.
Quoting percentages as though they were measured in service. They are model-scale or CFD figures at the design point and should be labelled as claims.

Getting the thrust fin mechanism wrong. The fin is HORIZONTAL, generates lift because the swirling flow meets it at an angle, and the FORWARD component of that lift is the recovered thrust. Fins are handed and set at opposite angles above and below the shaft line.
Saying an asymmetric rudder is asymmetric port-and-starboard for steering. It is asymmetric ABOVE AND BELOW the shaft line, because that is where the swirl reverses.
Presenting the Grim vane wheel as current equipment. The stem says 'currently in use' and honesty about its service record is worth more than pretending.
Forgetting that a fouled hull or a rough propeller erases the whole gain. Maintenance is the first energy saving measure.
Citing the 2018 Initial Strategy as the current IMO strategy. See the traps.

The operative IMO strategy at this sitting is the 2023 Strategy, MEPC.377(80), adopted 7 July 2023 - one month before this paper. The Initial Strategy of 2018 has been superseded. Note the direction of this trap: it is not a later paper importing later law, it is an EARLIER sitting of the identical question whose correct citation has gone stale in the seven months between January and August 2023.
EEXI and the operational CII are already applicable, not forthcoming - both since 1 January 2023. The revised Annex VI that carries them entered into force 1 November 2022.
The swirl reverses across the shaft line. Expect to be asked why the upper and lower fins are set at opposite angles. If they were set the same way, one pair would be a drag device.

The rudder bulb attacks a DIFFERENT loss from the other three. Fins, twist and the vane wheel all work on rotational energy; the bulb works on the hub vortex. That is why the bulb combines with the others and why they compete with each other.
The vane wheel takes no power from the engine. Expect 'where does its energy come from?' From the wasted rotational energy in the race, which drives the inner span as a turbine.
An asymmetric rudder is designed for one propeller and one direction of rotation. Expect to be asked whether you could fit the sister ship's rudder. Not if she turns the other way.
The cavitation benefit is often the real benefit. A rudder that stops eroding saves steel and off-hire whether or not the fuel saving materialises - and saying so is a mark for judgement.
Where exactly is the energy that these devices recover?
Why are rudder thrust fins horizontal and not vertical?
Your fins are fitted the wrong way up. What happens?
Why is a rudder bulb aligned with the propeller boss, and what happens if the gap is wrong?
The vane wheel takes no shaft power. So is it free energy?
Which of these four would you actually retrofit in a scheduled docking, and which would you not?
The maker claims six per cent. How would you find out whether you are getting it?
Your ship trades at 12 knots and the device was optimised at 15. What do you expect?
What would you do before spending anything on an energy saving device?

understand_first: A propeller pushes the ship forward, but it also leaves the water behind it spinning, and that spinning column is energy the engine paid for and the ship never got. There is a second waste right behind the middle of the propeller, where the boss stops abruptly and the water cannot close in behind it, so a tight whirlpool forms and sits there for the whole voyage. Now notice where the rudder is: it is standing directly in both of those, and it is the only big thing back there. So the idea behind every one of these devices is the same, and it is worth holding as a single sentence - put something in the wasted water and get a little of it back. A horizontal fin sitting in the spin meets it at an angle and, like any wing, produces lift; because the fin lies flat, part of that lift points forwards, which is thrust you did not pay for. Twisting the rudder itself does something subtler: the water is coming from one side above the shaft and the other side below it, so an ordinary flat rudder is being pushed sideways all the time even with the wheel amidships, and shaping each half to face its own flow simply stops that waste. A bulb on the rudder's nose fills the hole behind the boss so the whirlpool never forms. And the strangest of them is a free-spinning wheel that nothing drives - its inner part is turned by the spinning race like a windmill, and that rotation makes its outer part, which is out in still water, act as a small propeller. The two things to remember are the limits. Nothing here adds power - each device is only recovering a share of a waste that has a fixed size, so fitting three of them does not give you three times the saving, because they are all eating the same pie. And a dirty hull will swallow the whole gain, which is why cleaning comes before buying.

points: Quoted figures are model-scale or CFD at design draught, trim, speed, calm water and clean hull
Scale effects on wake and boundary layer flatter the model, and wake devices are where that error is largest
Combined-device gains are not additive
The ship rarely operates at the design point - trim, draught, fouling, weather, part load
Verify by continuous hull and propeller performance monitoring on ISO 19030, over enough time to separate the device from fouling
Ask for full-scale before-and-after data from a sister ship in a comparable trade

quick_revision.recall_15s: Three losses behind the propeller: swirl, hub vortex, rudder drag. The rudder is the only big thing standing in them. Fins - horizontal, lift from the swirl, forward component is thrust, HANDED. Asymmetric - twisted above and below the shaft because the swirl reverses; kills induced drag and cavitation. Bulb - fills the space behind the boss, suppresses the hub vortex, best retrofit. Vane wheel - turbine inboard, propeller outboard, no shaft power, ~10 per cent claimed but blade fatigue killed it. The gains do not add, and a dirty hull erases all of them.
quick_revision.critical_numbers: Thrust fins 2-5 per cent, asymmetric rudder 2-6 per cent, rudder bulb 2-5 per cent, Grim vane wheel about 10 per cent - all CLAIMS at design condition, none verified full scale, and they do not add. 1 January 2023 - EEXI and operational CII applicable. 7 July 2023 - the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, MEPC.377(80), one month before this sitting. 1 November 2022 - the revised MARPOL Annex VI in force.
quick_revision.critical_regulation: MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 as revised by MEPC.328(76) - EEXI and the operational CII, applicable from 1 January 2023. If you remember one thing about the regulation here, remember that it is the commercial reason these devices are being fitted at all: a permanent efficiency gain improves the attained EEXI and helps the annual rating, which is worth more than the fuel bill alone.
quick_revision.major_trap: Citing the Initial IMO Strategy of 2018 as the current IMO strategy. It was superseded on 7 July 2023 by the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, resolution MEPC.377(80) - one month before this sitting. Note the direction: the January 2023 sitting of this identical question cites the 2018 Strategy CORRECTLY for its own date, so the trap here is a stale citation from an EARLIER paper, not an imported one from a later paper.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the rudder efficiency question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 where the recoverable energy is; 2 thrust fins; 3 asymmetric rudders; 4 rudder bulbs; 5 Grim vane wheels; 6 what they have in common and why the gains do not add; 7 selection and retrofit; 8 judging whether a claimed gain is real. Each of steps 2 to 5 uses the same template: what it is, how it works, practical points, limitations.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What energy do rudder efficiency devices recover, and why the rudder?
retrieval_cards.answer: Two recoverable propeller losses: the rotational or swirl energy left in the race, which is the largest, and the hub vortex forming in the low-pressure core behind the boss. A third loss, separation and drag, is introduced by the rudder itself. The rudder is targeted because it is the only large appendage standing in the accelerated swirling slipstream, and it is already there and already structurally supported.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a rudder thrust fin produce thrust, and why are fins handed?
retrieval_cards.answer: The swirling inflow meets the horizontal fin at an angle of attack, so the fin develops lift like any aerofoil. Because the fin lies flat, the resolved component of that lift points forward, and that is recovered thrust. The swirl reverses across the shaft line - one direction above, the other below - so the upper and lower fins must be set at opposite angles. A fin fitted the wrong way up is a drag device.

retrieval_cards.prompt: In what sense is an asymmetric rudder asymmetric, and what does the asymmetry cure?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is asymmetric above and below the propeller shaft line, not port and starboard: the section is twisted or offset so each half faces its own local inflow. Because the swirl arrives from opposite sides above and below the shaft, a symmetrical rudder carries an incident angle over its whole span even with the helm amidships. Twisting removes that built-in incidence, cutting induced drag, separation and rudder cavitation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a Grim vane wheel work without taking shaft power?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is a freely rotating wheel of larger diameter than the propeller, connected to nothing. Its inner span lies inside the propeller race and is driven round as a turbine by the swirling flow; its outer span lies outside the race in undisturbed water and acts as a propeller, producing thrust. It converts wasted rotational energy into axial thrust and takes nothing from the engine.

retrieval_cards.prompt: You fit a bulb, fins and a twisted rudder, each claimed at 4 per cent. Do you get 12?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. All three are drawing on the same finite pool of wasted energy behind the propeller, so their gains are not additive - and three of the four devices in this family attack the same loss, rotational swirl. Only the bulb attacks a different one, the hub vortex, which is why it combines with the others better than they combine with each other. A combined arrangement must be designed and tested as one system.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Are Grim vane wheels current equipment?
retrieval_cards.answer: Largely not, and the stem asks about devices currently in use, so say so. Claimed gains reached about 10 per cent, the highest of the four, and ships were fitted in the 1980s. The outer blade span is long, slender and lightly supported in a highly unsteady flow, and blade fatigue, blade loss and bearing problems on the free-running hub ended its use. It is examined because it shows the principle in its purest form.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The maker claims six per cent. How do you find out whether you are getting it?
retrieval_cards.answer: Treat the figure as a model-scale or CFD result at design draught, trim and speed in calm water with a clean hull. Verify by continuous hull and propeller performance monitoring - shaft power against speed through water corrected for displacement, trim and weather - on ISO 19030, over long enough to separate the device's effect from fouling. Ask for full-scale before-and-after data from a sister ship in a comparable trade.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which IMO strategy is operative at an August 2023 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: The 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, resolution MEPC.377(80), adopted at MEPC 80 on 7 July 2023 - one month earlier. NOT the Initial Strategy of 2018, which it superseded. The January 2023 sitting of this identical question cites the 2018 Strategy correctly for its own date, so this is a stale citation inherited from an earlier paper rather than a later one imported.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A four-limb technical question that looks like a recall exercise and is not. The examiner is testing whether the candidate understands that all four named devices are recovering from the same small set of propeller losses, because a candidate who has that idea can explain a device he has never seen and can also say why the claimed gains do not add. The second discriminator is scepticism: the stem invites brochure percentages, and an answer that recites them without qualification tells the examiner that the candidate has not thought about where the numbers come from.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: Sixteen marks with no printed split on this copy, and none on the January 2023 sitting of the same stem either. The four limbs are named equally and are treated equally - one section each - but they are not the whole question: the stem opens with a proposition about propulsion effectiveness and asks for devices 'currently in use', which licenses the loss-budget section that precedes them and the honesty about the vane wheel that follows. The answer allots one section to the losses, four to the named devices, and three to synthesis, selection and verification.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the swirl and the hub vortex are identified as the recoverable losses before any device is named. That the thrust fin mechanism is given correctly - horizontal fin, lift from the swirl, forward component - and that the handedness is explained. That the asymmetry of an asymmetric rudder is placed above and below the shaft line and not port and starboard. That the bulb is tied to the hub vortex specifically. That the vane wheel's turbine-and-propeller action is explained and its service record stated honestly. And that the answer ends on whether a claimed gain can be believed.
decomposition_gate.primary_source_plan: Build the technical content on the MIW verification record for QP2301 Q1, the earlier same-year sitting of this identical stem, corroborated against QP2404 Q4, QP2409 Q9 and QP2506 Q1. Take the loss-budget framing from QP2304 Q6 and QP2502 Q8, and the fouling argument from QP2503 Q8. Re-establish the regulatory context for August 2023 rather than inheriting it, the donor's 2018 Initial Strategy citation having been superseded on 7 July 2023. Deliberately NOT planned: any quotation of MARPOL Annex VI text, the corpus being citation-ready only; any clause of ISO 19030, which is not held; any class rule number; and any percentage presented as verified service data.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW - but not zero, and the residual risk runs in an unusual direction. The physics does not date. The single moving part is the IMO strategy citation, and the trap is that the EARLIER same-year donor carries a citation that was correct in January 2023 and had been superseded by August 2023. An earlier donor cannot import later law; it can carry superseded law, and this question is the paper's one example of it.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. The subject is naval architecture and no national law is engaged. The only boundary to keep straight is between MARPOL Annex VI, which is mandatory, the IMO GHG Strategy, which is policy and not a rule, and ISO 19030 and class requirements, which are industry and contractual standards. An answer that describes the Strategy as a regulation, or ISO 19030 as mandatory, has the levels wrong.
decomposition_gate.technical_ambiguities: 'Currently in use' is the ambiguity that matters. Three of the four devices are in current use and the fourth substantially is not, and the answer says so rather than treating them as equals - which is a judgement, not a fact, and is recorded as one. 'Rudder-efficiency improvements devices/ techniques' is also loose: read narrowly it means devices on the rudder, read widely it would take in ducts, boss cap fins and pre-swirl stators. The answer is confined to the rudder side, because that is what the four named limbs are, but the propeller-side family is named in one sentence so the boundary is visible.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Eight numbered sections. A bulleted loss budget first. Then four parallel device sections, each following the same what / how / practical / limitations template so the marker can find them and the candidate can reproduce them under pressure. A bulleted synthesis section carrying the non-additivity proposition. A bulleted selection section written from the Chief Engineer's position. A bulleted verification section. A closing single-sentence proposition.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That the operative IMO strategy at an August 2023 sitting is the 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, resolution MEPC.377(80) of 7 July 2023, and not the Initial Strategy of 2018.
reverify_before_publication.why: The reversal on this question runs FORWARD, which is the direction a reviewer will not expect. The wording donor QP2301-Q1 is an EARLIER same-year paper and cites the 2018 Initial Strategy correctly for January 2023. A reviewer comparing the two same-year papers will see a discrepancy and may reconcile them the wrong way. The 2023 Strategy was adopted one month before this sitting and is the correct citation here.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The percentage gain ranges quoted for each device - about 2 to 5 per cent for thrust fins and rudder bulbs, 2 to 6 per cent for asymmetric rudders, and about 10 per cent claimed for the Grim vane wheel.
reverify_before_publication.why: None is verified against full-scale service data and published ranges are wide and inconsistent. They are given in the answer as CLAIMS at design condition and the answer devotes a section to why such figures flatter. Recorded as an accepted limitation rather than removed, because a candidate asked for an order of magnitude in the oral needs one.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That Grim vane wheels are rare in service today, blade fatigue, blade loss and bearing problems having ended their use.
reverify_before_publication.why: This is a statement about service history carried from MIW's own records rather than from a survey of the fleet, and it is a judgement that the stem's phrase 'currently in use' requires the answer to make. It is stated as service experience, not as a count of ships.

regulations: Resolution MEPC.377(80) - the 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, adopted 7 July 2023 at MEPC 80; the operative IMO strategy at this sitting

MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 as revised by resolution MEPC.328(76) - the Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index and the operational Carbon Intensity Indicator, applicable from 1 January 2023; context and commercial driver only
ISO 19030 - measurement of changes in hull and propeller performance; the industry standard by which a claimed gain is verified in service. Named only, not read

Classification society approval of the attachment, local scantlings and fatigue assessment of a retrofitted appendage, and reassessment of rudder cavitation after modification. Described by principle; no rule number cited
